rv.q: It’s a pleasurable escape, for a tuneful two-plus hours, into a quasi-cartoon version of old New York, where the virtuous struggle and the villainous thrive.
It's mostly good, silly fun from then on, buoyed by a talented cast of 12—they're an entertaining lot—and a six-piece band that includes a harp.
The artful welding of style and entertainment warrant many weeks, no, months of deserved bows for Ms. Moore and her tremendous troupe.
Perhaps it’s the Christmas story we actually need this year.
When's the last time you left a new musical humming the score? If you've seen The Streets of New York at the Irish Repertory Theatre, you're probably humming to beat the band.

The Streets of New York, a musical revival adapted from Dion Boucicault's 1857 play The Poor of New York, is a festive production full of melodramatic storytelling and poppy tunes delivered with merriment by an unforgettable cast.
It is two hours of pure entertainment.
On a small space and with limited resources, each moment is brought to life.
It appears the cast is having just as much fun as the audience in this beautifully wrapped gift for the holiday season.

cn.t: Critics praise this festive musical revival as pure entertainment, with Charlotte Moore's melodious songs and light directorial touch bringing Boucicault's 19th-century melodrama to vibrant life through spirited performances and poppy tunes.
